title: This is all that’s left of a giant star
caption: Part of the Vela supernova remnant, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
celestial: Vela Supernova Remnant · about 800 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO/VPHAS+ team. Acknowledgement: Cambridge Astronomical Survey Unit

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Intricate, thread-like structures of glowing gas fill this view of the Vela supernova remnant. They are what remains after a massive star blew itself apart in a powerful explosion around 11 000 years ago.

In a supernova, shock waves ripple out through the surrounding gas and compress it into fine threads. Energy released by the explosion then heats those threads until they shine brightly. The patterns in this picture are the result.

The image is only a small part of a much larger picture made by the VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM instrument, hosted at ESO's Paranal Observatory. The Vela remnant is only 800 light-years from Earth, making it one of the closest examples of such an explosion. Being so near, it can be studied in great detail, helping astronomers learn what happens as massive stars come to the end of their lives.
scale: The source lists a distance of 800 light years, so the light in this picture set out roughly 800 years ago.

understand.summary: This image was made with OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope. The source doesn't give the filters or say what the colors represent.
understand.eye: The telescope's wide-field camera gathers far more light than the eye can.
